body:
MAIN AUDIT: CLEAN. f49d72d, tree 9b87540, GATE_EXIT=0, 17 suite totals, 1370 tests, 0 errors, 0
failures. Full compileAll + testJVM + scalafmtCheckAll on main ITSELF, not on a candidate.

WHY I RAN IT. FORTY-FOUR MERGES LANDED ON MAIN TODAY. Every one was gated against a merged tree --
main-plus-candidate at the moment I gated it -- and that is the right court for admitting a
candidate. But it is a court on a PAIR. Nobody had gated the ACCUMULATION, and interactions between
merges that landed within minutes of each other are exactly what a sequence of pairwise gates does
not cover.

They are clean. Whatever else today produced, it did not produce accumulated drift.

WHAT THIS ESTABLISHES: main compiles and its JVM tests pass AS AN INDEPENDENT WHOLE. That is a
different claim from "each merge was green when it landed", and it is the one nobody had made.

WHAT IT DOES NOT ESTABLISH, stated so nobody over-reads it:
  - JS and Native are UNMEASURED. This was testJVM. Several of today's landings touched
    cross-platform code and authors gated those themselves, but I did not.
  - It says nothing about whether any individual merge was CORRECT. A wrong-but-consistent change
    passes this exactly as a right one does.
  - It is a snapshot of f49d72d. It expires the moment the next thing lands.

I am adding this to my own routine rather than filing it: A PERIODIC AUDIT OF MAIN ITSELF, not of
a candidate. The merge gate protects each admission; nothing was protecting the sum. That is a gap
in the procedure I built, and it existed all day without anyone noticing because every individual
answer was green.

Also recorded the sweep-2 slice status on bd-01M16WATA75CBRRB9X9ZKJF2MS so the state is in one
place: A and B landed, C and D1 held by actors silent since 15:06, D2 sequenced behind E, E blocked
twice over. Two in, four out.
